chapter_note.about: A perceptron is the simplest neural unit: it multiplies the inputs by weights, adds a bias and answers yes or no with one straight-line boundary. This chapter covers what that boundary can and cannot do, the rule that learns the weights from mistakes, how to count the parameters of a layered network, why layers need a non-linear bend to be useful, how hidden units cut the plane into regions so that XOR works, and when the learning rule is guaranteed to stop.

chapter_note.simple: A perceptron is a tiny decision maker. It scores an item by adding up its numbers, each times a weight, and says yes if the score is positive. On a graph, that means one straight line splits yes from no. It learns by being corrected: each time it is wrong, it nudges its weights toward the right answer. It can only learn rules a single ruler line can draw, so XOR defeats it. Stacking several perceptrons into layers lets the network combine many lines, but only if something bends the signal between the layers, otherwise the layers collapse into one. In exam words: a perceptron computes $\operatorname{sign}(w^\top x+b)$, updates on mistakes, converges only on separable data, and a multilayer network needs non-linear activations.

cards.title: Perceptron and linear separability
cards.simple: A perceptron is a very simple judge. It looks at a few numbers about an item, multiplies each by a weight, adds a starting bonus called the bias, and says yes if the total is positive and no if it is not. On a graph, this judge cuts the page with one straight line, with yes on one side and no on the other. So it can only learn rules that a ruler can draw. AND and OR work. XOR, where yes means exactly one of the two inputs is on, would need a bent line, so it fails. In exam words: $\hat y=\operatorname{sign}(w^\top x+b)$ has a hyperplane boundary, so it handles only linearly separable data.
cards.idea: A **perceptron** is the simplest neuron. It computes a score $f(x)=w^\top x+b$ and outputs $+1$ if the score is positive and $-1$ otherwise. The set of points with score exactly 0 is a straight line (a plane in more dimensions), so the perceptron can only separate classes that a line can separate. AND and OR are separable. XOR is not.
cards.definition:
$$\hat y=\operatorname{sign}(w^\top x+b),\qquad \text{boundary: } w^\top x+b=0$$

Symbols: $w$ is the weight vector, $b$ is the bias and $x$ the input. $w$ points at a right angle to the boundary, toward the $+1$ side. GATE uses the convention $\operatorname{sign}(0)=-1$, so a point exactly on the line is classified as $-1$.
cards.intuition_full: The score $f$ is a weighted vote. Each input pushes the total up or down by its weight times its value, and the bias shifts the whole thing. The class changes exactly when the total crosses 0, which is the line $w^\top x+b=0$. A bigger $b$ moves the line away from the origin. A different $w$ rotates it. Why can it not do XOR? XOR says yes for $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ and no for $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$. The two yes points sit on one diagonal and the two no points on the other. Any line that puts both yes points on one side must also catch the midpoint of the two, which is $(0.5,0.5)$, the midpoint of the no points too. So the sides cannot be separated. This is the same overlapping rubber band argument as on the SVM separability card. The algebra on the GATE-level example shows the same thing with four inequalities.

examples.setup: A perceptron has $w=(2,1)$ and $b=-4$. Find the output for $A=(1,1)$, $B=(3,1)$ and $C=(1,3)$, and describe the boundary.
steps: The score is $f(x)=2x_1+x_2-4$. The boundary $f=0$ is the line $2x_1+x_2=4$. It crosses the axes at $(2,0)$ and $(0,4)$. $w=(2,1)$ points toward the $+1$ side.
$A=(1,1)$: $f=2+1-4=-1$. Negative, so the output is $-1$.
$B=(3,1)$: $f=6+1-4=3$. Positive, so the output is $+1$.
$C=(1,3)$: $f=2+3-4=1$. Positive, so the output is $+1$.
The line splits the plane into two half-planes. $B$ and $C$ are on the side $w$ points to, and $A$ is on the other.

examples.setup: Inputs are in $\{0,1\}^2$. XOR outputs $+1$ for $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ and $-1$ for $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$. Show that no perceptron $\operatorname{sign}(w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b)$ computes XOR. Use $\operatorname{sign}(0)=-1$.
steps: $(0,0)\to-1$ needs $f\le0$, so $b\le0$.
Add the two inequalities from step 2: $w_1+w_2+2b>0$.
Subtract the inequality of step 3: $(w_1+w_2+2b)-(w_1+w_2+b)=b$. The left side is greater than $0$ and the subtracted term is at most $0$, so $b>0$. That contradicts $b\le0$.
examples.answer: The four conditions cannot all hold, so no perceptron computes XOR. AND and OR have solutions, for example $w=(2,2)$ with $b=-3$ for AND.

examples.setup: For $w=(2,1)$ and $b=-4$, what is the output at $x=(1,2)$?
steps: $f=2\cdot1+1\cdot2-4=0$. The point is exactly on the boundary.
With the GATE convention $\operatorname{sign}(0)=-1$, the output is $-1$.
examples.answer: $-1$. Points on the line go to the negative class. Other books use $+1$ or call it undefined, so follow the convention stated in the question.

cards.title: Perceptron learning rule
cards.simple: The perceptron learns like a student who is corrected only when wrong. It tries an example. If its answer is right, it does nothing. If it is wrong, it nudges its line toward the right answer: for a missed yes it adds the example to its weights, and for a missed no it subtracts it. The nudge always pushes that example's score the right way, by a known amount: the example's squared length plus 1. One nudge may or may not fully fix the mistake, but the score always improves. In exam words: on a mistake ($y\,f(x)\le0$) set $w\leftarrow w+yx$ and $b\leftarrow b+y$, and then $yf$ rises by $\|x\|^2+1$.
cards.idea: The perceptron learns from its **mistakes**. A mistake is an example whose score has the wrong sign, $y\,f(x)\le0$. On a mistake, add $y$ times the example to the weights and $y$ to the bias. Right answers cause no change. After one update the score of that example always moves in the right direction by exactly $\|x\|^2+1$.
cards.definition:
$$\text{if } y\,f(x)\le0:\quad w\leftarrow w+y\,x,\quad b\leftarrow b+y\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad y\,f_{\text{new}}(x)=y\,f_{\text{old}}(x)+\|x\|^2+1$$

Symbols: $y\in\{+1,-1\}$ is the label. $f(x)=w^\top x+b$ is the score. $\|x\|^2=x_1^2+x_2^2+\cdots$ is the squared length of the input. The extra $+1$ comes from the bias update.
cards.intuition_full: Why does adding $yx$ help? Take a missed $+1$ example. Its score is too low. Adding $x$ to $w$ makes the new weights point more toward $x$, so the dot product $w^\top x$ grows by $x^\top x=\|x\|^2$. The bias update adds $y=1$ to the score. So the score rises by $\|x\|^2+1$. For a missed $-1$ example, subtracting $x$ lowers $w^\top x$ by $\|x\|^2$ and the bias lowers the score by 1. So $f$ falls by $\|x\|^2+1$ and $yf=-f$ rises by the same amount. In both cases the quantity $yf$ goes up by $\|x\|^2+1$, which is always at least 1. One update may not be enough to make $yf$ positive, but repeated updates on the same point will. A fix for one point can break another, so the algorithm cycles through the data. The next card says when this stops. A learning rate $\eta$ simply scales the step: $w\leftarrow w+\eta yx$ and $yf$ then rises by $\eta(\|x\|^2+1)$.

examples.setup: A perceptron has $w=(1,-1)$ and $b=0$. It sees $x=(1,3)$ with label $y=+1$. Apply one update and find the new score.
steps: Start: $f(x)=x_1-x_2$. The rule on a mistake: $w\leftarrow w+yx$ and $b\leftarrow b+y$.
$f(1,3)=1-3=-2$, so $yf=-2\le0$. This is a mistake.
New score: $f(1,3)=2\cdot1+2\cdot3+1=9$. $yf$ rose from $-2$ to $9$, a rise of $11=\|x\|^2+1=1+9+1$.
examples.answer: New $w=(2,2)$, $b=1$, and the score of $x$ is $9$. The increase of $11$ equals $\|x\|^2+1$.

examples.setup: A perceptron has $w=(2,1)$ and $b=-1$. It sees $x=(2,3)$ with label $y=-1$. Is it a mistake? Apply the update and find how $y f$ changes.
steps: $f=2\cdot2+1\cdot3-1=6$. With $y=-1$: $yf=-6\le0$. A mistake.
Update: $w\leftarrow w+yx=(2,1)-(2,3)=(0,-2)$ and $b\leftarrow b+y=-1-1=-2$.
New score: $f=0\cdot2+(-2)\cdot3-2=-8$. So $yf=8$.
$yf$ went from $-6$ to $8$, a rise of $14=\|x\|^2+1=4+9+1$.
examples.answer: A mistake. New $w=(0,-2)$, $b=-2$, $f=-8$. The quantity $yf$ rises by $14=\|x\|^2+1$. The rule works the same for $y=-1$: the score falls by $\|x\|^2+1$.

examples.setup: Repeat the basic example with a small learning rate $\eta=0.1$: $w\leftarrow w+\eta yx$ and $b\leftarrow b+\eta y$. Is the point fixed after one update?
steps: The rise is $-0.9-(-2)=1.1=\eta(\|x\|^2+1)=0.1\cdot11$. The score is still negative.
examples.answer: No. $yf$ is still $-0.9$, so the point is still a mistake. The score improved by $0.1\times11=1.1$. A small step needs several updates.

cards.title: Counting parameters
cards.simple: Counting parameters is bookkeeping. Every arrow between two layers of neurons carries one adjustable number, called a weight. Every neuron after the inputs usually has one more adjustable number, its bias, like a starting score. So for each layer you multiply the number of neurons before it by the number in it to count the arrows, then add one bias per neuron. Add up all the layers. The neurons themselves are not parameters, only the arrows and the biases. In exam words: a layer $n_{in}\to n_{out}$ has $n_{in}n_{out}$ weights plus $n_{out}$ biases.
cards.idea: The **parameters** of a network are the numbers it learns: one **weight** for every connection and one **bias** for every neuron after the inputs. To count them layer by layer, multiply the sizes of two neighbouring layers for the weights, then add the size of the later layer for the biases. Add all the layers together. Neurons and activation functions are not counted.
cards.definition:
$$\#\text{params}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\big(n_{\ell-1}\,n_{\ell}+n_{\ell}\big)\qquad\text{(drop the }+n_\ell\text{ if there are no biases)}$$

Symbols: $n_0$ is the number of inputs and $n_1,\dots,n_L$ are the sizes of the later layers. $n_{\ell-1}n_\ell$ counts the arrows into layer $\ell$. $n_\ell$ counts its biases. The input layer has no weights or biases of its own.
cards.intuition_full: Draw the network and count with your eyes. Every arrow is a weight, because each arrow multiplies the signal passing along it by a learnable number. Every neuron after the inputs adds one constant to its total before the activation, and that constant is the bias. Between two fully connected layers every neuron on the left connects to every neuron on the right, so the arrows number $n_{\ell-1}\times n_\ell$. A phrase like '4 inputs, one hidden layer of 5 and 3 outputs' has 3 layers of neurons but only 2 layers of weights. A common slip is to count neurons or to give the input layer a bias. Sigmoid, ReLU and softmax have no parameters in the usual textbook network. Read the question for two switches: whether biases are used, and whether some layer is said to have none.

examples.setup: A fully connected network has 2 inputs, one hidden layer of 3 units and 1 output unit. Every unit after the inputs has a bias. How many learnable parameters does it have?
steps: Layers: $2\to3\to1$. There are two layers of weights.
Layer 1 weights: $2\times3=6$.
Layer 1 biases: one per hidden unit, $3$. Layer 1 total $=6+3=9$.
Layer 2 weights: $3\times1=3$. Layer 2 bias: $1$. Layer 2 total $=4$.
Total $=9+4=13$. The 6 neurons are not what we count.

examples.setup: A fully connected network has layer sizes $12\to9\to6\to3$. Count the parameters with biases at every neuron, and without any biases.
steps: There are three weight layers: $12\to9$, $9\to6$ and $6\to3$.
Biases: one per non-input neuron, $9+6+3=18$.
With biases: $180+18=198$. Without biases: $180$.
examples.answer: 198 with biases and 180 without. Check the question for the bias switch.

examples.setup: Layer sizes $6\to4\to4\to2$. The hidden layers have biases, but the output layer has none. How many parameters?
steps: $4\to2$ with no bias: $4\times2=8$.
examples.answer: 56. Count the bias term layer by layer, so a missing bias in one layer is easy to handle.

cards.why: GATE DA asks one parameter-count NAT in almost every paper. It is quick and sure marks if you do it layer by layer. In GATE: layer sizes with or without biases, sometimes with a layer described in words.
how: Write the layer sizes in a row, input first.
For each neighbouring pair multiply the two sizes. That is the weights.
Add the size of the later layer if biases are used.
Add all the layers. Do not count neurons or the input layer's biases.
cards.mistake: Counting neurons instead of connections, forgetting the biases, or adding biases when the question says there are none. Write the bias term separately for each layer.
edge_cases: A layer with no bias contributes only $n_{in}n_{out}$.
The input layer has no parameters.
Activation functions such as sigmoid and ReLU have no parameters.
A network with no hidden layer, 3 inputs and 1 output with bias, has $3+1=4$ parameters, the same as logistic regression.

Symbols: $n_0$ is the number of inputs and $n_1,\dots,n_L$ are the sizes of the later layers. $n_{\ell-1}n_\ell$ counts the arrows into layer $\ell$. $n_\ell$ counts its biases. The input layer has no weights or biases of its own.

**Worked example.** A fully connected network has 2 inputs, one hidden layer of 3 units and 1 output unit. Every unit after the inputs has a bias. How many learnable parameters does it have?

1. Layers: $2\to3\to1$. There are two layers of weights.
2. Layer 1 weights: $2\times3=6$.
3. Layer 1 biases: one per hidden unit, $3$. Layer 1 total $=6+3=9$.
4. Layer 2 weights: $3\times1=3$. Layer 2 bias: $1$. Layer 2 total $=4$.
5. Total $=9+4=13$. The 6 neurons are not what we count.

**Answer:** 13 parameters (9 weights and 4 biases).

cards.title: Why hidden layers need a non-linearity
cards.simple: Imagine one machine that multiplies by 2 and another that multiplies by 3. Join them and you get one machine that multiplies by 6. Layers that only multiply and add (linear layers) behave the same way: stack ten and you still have one linear machine. A layer only adds power if something bends the signal in between, such as a ReLU, which turns negative numbers into 0. That bend is called a non-linearity, and it is why a deep network can learn curved boundaries. In exam words: with identity activations, $W_2(W_1x)=(W_2W_1)x$ is one linear map.
cards.idea: A stack of **linear layers** is just one linear layer. If the activation is the identity, two layers $W_2(W_1x)$ equal the single layer $(W_2W_1)x$, and a hundred layers are still one. A **non-linear activation** such as a threshold, sigmoid or ReLU between the layers is what gives a network extra power, such as computing XOR or drawing curved boundaries.
cards.definition:
$$W_2(W_1x)=(W_2W_1)\,x\qquad\text{and with biases}\qquad W_2(W_1x+b_1)+b_2=(W_2W_1)x+(W_2b_1+b_2)$$

Symbols: $W_1,W_2$ are weight matrices, $b_1,b_2$ are bias vectors. The product $P=W_2W_1$ is one matrix. A non-linear $\sigma$ in between, $W_2\,\sigma(W_1x)$, cannot be written as a single matrix times $x$.
cards.intuition_full: Matrix multiplication can be regrouped: doing $W_1$ first and then $W_2$ is the same as doing the combined matrix $W_2W_1$ once. That is a fact about linearity, not about networks. A linear layer can stretch, rotate and shear space, but it can never fold it. Folding needs a bend. The ReLU $\max(0,z)$ is the simplest bend: it keeps positive numbers and sets negative numbers to 0. For an input where every hidden score is positive, the ReLU does nothing and the network acts like one matrix. But the set of such inputs is a region bounded by lines, and in each region the matrix is different. The network is therefore made of several linear pieces glued together, which is more flexible than any single matrix. Notice also what is lost without the bend: the hidden layer has many weights, but they all merge into the entries of $P$. A $4\to3\to2$ linear network has 18 weights but acts like a single $2\times4$ matrix with 8.

examples.setup: A network has two layers with identity activations. $W_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $W_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\end{pmatrix}$. For $x=(2,1)$ compute the output layer by layer, then with the single matrix $P=W_2W_1$. Then put a ReLU on the hidden layer and use $x=(1,2)$.
steps: The network computes $h=W_1x$ and then $y=W_2h$ with no bend in between.
Multiply the matrices: $P=W_2W_1=(1\cdot1+2\cdot1,\ 1\cdot1+2\cdot(-1))=(3,\,-1)$. Then $Px=3\cdot2-1\cdot1=5$. Same answer.
So two linear layers are one linear layer with weights $(3,-1)$. More linear layers add no power.
With a ReLU and $x=(1,2)$: $h=W_1x=(3,-1)$ becomes $(3,0)$. $y=1\cdot3+2\cdot0=3$. The single map gives $Px=3\cdot1-1\cdot2=1$. They differ.
examples.answer: Without the bend, the network equals $P=(3,-1)$ and gives 5 at $(2,1)$. With a ReLU the output at $(1,2)$ is 3, not 1, so the network is no longer one linear map.

examples.setup: A network $4\to3\to2$ has identity activations and no biases. How many weights does it have, and how many weights does the equivalent single layer need?
steps: Weights: $4\times3+3\times2=12+6=18$.
$W_1$ is $3\times4$ and $W_2$ is $2\times3$. The product $W_2W_1$ is $2\times4$, which has $2\times4=8$ entries.
Any function the network computes is $x\mapsto(W_2W_1)x$, so 8 weights are enough.
With biases the combined bias is $W_2b_1+b_2$, only 2 numbers.
examples.answer: 18 weights in the network, but it is equivalent to a single layer with 8. The hidden layer adds redundancy and no power.

examples.setup: Use the basic network with a ReLU on the hidden layer. Is the output at $x=(2,1)$ different from the single-matrix answer?
steps: $h=W_1x=(3,1)$. Both entries are positive, so ReLU leaves them unchanged.
$y=1\cdot3+2\cdot1=5$, the same as $Px=5$.
examples.answer: No, they agree at $(2,1)$. A ReLU network behaves like one matrix wherever all its hidden scores are positive. The difference appears only across the lines where a hidden score changes sign, as at $(1,2)$.

cards.title: Hidden units as half-planes
cards.simple: Each hidden unit with a threshold draws one straight line on the page and says which side an item is on. Two units draw two lines, so the page now has up to four areas. The output unit looks at what the hidden units said and decides what to answer for each area. XOR needs a strip in the middle to say no and both outer corners to say yes. Two lines make that strip, and the output says yes if either line fired. So a hidden layer is a set of cuts, and the output combines them. In exam words: each hidden threshold unit is a half-plane, and $k$ lines cut the plane into at most $(k^2+k+2)/2$ regions.
cards.idea: A hidden unit with a threshold activation, $h=[w^\top x+b>0]$, splits the input plane into two **half-planes** with one line. A layer of $k$ such units draws $k$ lines and cuts the plane into regions. The output unit combines the hidden answers, so a network can say yes to a union of regions. This is how two hidden units solve XOR, which no single line can.
cards.definition:
$$h_j=[\,w_j^\top x+b_j>0\,],\qquad \text{regions from } k \text{ lines in general position}=\frac{k^2+k+2}{2}$$

Symbols: $[\cdot]$ is 1 when the statement inside is true and 0 otherwise. 'General position' means no two lines are parallel and no three lines meet at one point. The output unit sees only the vector $(h_1,\dots,h_k)$, so it can tell apart only the regions that give different vectors.
cards.intuition_full: Think of each hidden unit as a straight fence across the field, with one side marked 1 and the other 0. Each point of the field gets a code of 0s and 1s, one for each fence. Points in the same region have the same code. The output unit works only from these codes. So the network can only label whole regions. For XOR, two fences make three useful regions: a strip between them and two outer corners. The strip carries code $(0,0)$ and the outer corners carry $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. The output unit says yes unless the code is $(0,0)$. How many regions can $k$ fences make? Add the lines one at a time. The $j$-th line crosses the $j-1$ earlier lines at $j-1$ points. Those points split it into $j$ pieces, and each piece cuts one old region in two, so it adds $j$ regions. Hence $1+(1+2+\cdots+k)=\frac{k^2+k+2}{2}$. Parallel or concurrent lines make fewer regions. With enough hidden units a one-hidden-layer network can approximate any reasonable function, which is the universal approximation idea.

examples.setup: A network has two hidden threshold units $h_1=[x_1-x_2>0.5]$ and $h_2=[x_2-x_1>0.5]$ and an output $[h_1+h_2>0.5]$. Evaluate it on the four inputs $(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)$.
steps: Output: $h_1+h_2=0,1,1,0$. Compare with $0.5$: the output is $0,1,1,0$.
The two lines make a strip. $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ sit inside it and $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ sit outside on opposite sides.
examples.answer: The outputs are $0,1,1,0$, which is XOR. Two hidden units and an output unit compute a function that no single perceptron can.

examples.setup: A hidden layer has 4 threshold units in a 2D input space. The four lines are in general position. What is the greatest number of regions the plane is cut into?
steps: One line cuts the plane into $2$ regions.
A second line crosses the first at $1$ point, so it splits into 2 pieces and adds $2$ regions: $2+2=4$.
A third line crosses the two earlier lines at 2 points, so it has 3 pieces and adds $3$: $4+3=7$.
A fourth line crosses 3 lines, has 4 pieces and adds $4$: $7+4=11$.
examples.answer: 11 regions. The 4 hidden units can give at most 11 different codes out of the $2^4=16$ possible 0/1 patterns.

examples.setup: The three hidden lines are all parallel. How many regions do they make?
steps: Parallel lines never cross, so each new line adds only one region, not more.
$k$ parallel lines cut the plane into $k+1$ strips, so $3+1=4$ regions, not 7.
examples.answer: 4 regions. The bound $(k^2+k+2)/2$ needs general position. Parallel or concurrent lines give fewer.

cards.title: Convergence of the perceptron
cards.simple: The perceptron learns by being corrected whenever it is wrong. If one straight line can separate the two groups, it keeps nudging until every point is right, and then it stops for good. How many corrections can it need? A wide gap between the groups and points that are not spread too far from the centre mean few corrections. A narrow gap with a huge spread means many. If no straight line works, as with XOR, it never settles and keeps nudging forever. In exam words: it converges if and only if the data are linearly separable, and it makes at most $(R/\gamma)^2$ mistakes.
cards.idea: The perceptron algorithm **stops after finitely many updates if and only if the data are linearly separable**. When they are, the number of mistakes is at most $(R/\gamma)^2$. $R$ is the length of the longest input vector and $\gamma$ is the margin of a separating plane. A wide margin and a small spread mean few mistakes. On non-separable data, such as XOR, it never stops.
cards.definition:
$$\#\text{mistakes}\ \le\ \Big(\frac{R}{\gamma}\Big)^2,\qquad R=\max_i\|x_i\|,\qquad \gamma=\min_i\ y_i\,(w^{*\top}x_i)\ \ \text{with}\ \|w^*\|=1$$

Symbols: $w^*$ is any unit vector that separates the data (the bound is stated for a plane through the origin). $\gamma$ is the distance of the closest point from that plane. $R$ is how far the farthest point is from the origin.
cards.intuition_full: Why does it stop? Each update pushes the weight vector toward $w^*$. After $k$ updates the dot product $w^\top w^*$ has grown by at least $\gamma$ each time, so it is at least $k\gamma$. At the same time the length of $w$ cannot grow fast: each update adds at most $R^2$ to $\|w\|^2$ because the update happens only on a mistake, when the step does not increase it by more than $\|x\|^2$. So $\|w\|^2\le kR^2$. Since $w^\top w^*\le\|w\|$ (the dot product with a unit vector is at most the length), we get $k\gamma\le\sqrt k\,R$, which means $k\le(R/\gamma)^2$. In words, the weights keep turning toward $w^*$ but cannot grow quickly, so the number of steps is capped. If the data are not separable there is no $w^*$, the argument fails, and the algorithm cycles. Note what is absent from the bound: the number of points and the number of dimensions. Another fact: multiplying all inputs by a constant multiplies $R$ and $\gamma$ by the same constant, so the bound does not change.

examples.setup: Class $+1$ at $(3,2)$ and $(-1,4)$, class $-1$ at $(2,-1)$ and $(-3,-2)$. The unit vector $w^*=(0,1)$ separates them (no bias). Find the perceptron mistake bound.
steps: $w^*=(0,1)$ has length 1. The plane is the line $x_2=0$. The $+$ points are above it and the $-$ points below.
Margins $y\,w^{*\top}x$: $1\cdot2=2$, $1\cdot4=4$, $(-1)(-1)=1$, $(-1)(-2)=2$. The smallest is $\gamma=1$.
Lengths $\|x\|$: $\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13}$, $\sqrt{1+16}=\sqrt{17}$, $\sqrt{4+1}=\sqrt5$, $\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13}$. The largest is $R=\sqrt{17}\approx4.12$.
So at most 17 updates happen, whatever order the points come in.
examples.answer: At most $(R/\gamma)^2=17$ mistakes. A bound, not an exact count: the real number can be smaller.

examples.setup: A separable data set has $R=6$ and $\gamma=0.5$. Every input is now halved, $x\to x/2$. What happens to the mistake bound?
steps: Halving every input halves every length, so $R=3$. It also halves every distance to the plane, so $\gamma=0.25$.
examples.answer: The bound stays 144. Rescaling the inputs changes $R$ and $\gamma$ by the same factor, so $R/\gamma$ does not change.

examples.setup: In the first example a student uses $w^*=(0,2)$, which separates the data too. They compute $\gamma$ with it and get a different bound. What went wrong?
steps: Using $\gamma=2$ gives $(\sqrt{17}/2)^2=17/4=4.25$. That is too small.
The bound needs a unit vector. $\|w^*\|=2$, so divide: $\gamma=2/2=1$ and the bound is 17 again.
examples.answer: The student forgot to normalise $w^*$. With a unit vector the bound is 17, not 4.25. Any separating vector must be rescaled to length 1 first.

Take a unit separating vector $w^*$ and compute $\gamma=\min_i y_i\,w^{*\top}x_i$.
Compute $R=\max_i\|x_i\|$.

cards.what: The perceptron algorithm **stops after finitely many updates if and only if the data are linearly separable**. When they are, the number of mistakes is at most $(R/\gamma)^2$. $R$ is the length of the longest input vector and $\gamma$ is the margin of a separating plane. A wide margin and a small spread mean few mistakes. On non-separable data, such as XOR, it never stops.
cards.what_full:
The perceptron algorithm **stops after finitely many updates if and only if the data are linearly separable**. When they are, the number of mistakes is at most $(R/\gamma)^2$. $R$ is the length of the longest input vector and $\gamma$ is the margin of a separating plane. A wide margin and a small spread mean few mistakes. On non-separable data, such as XOR, it never stops.

$$\#\text{mistakes}\ \le\ \Big(\frac{R}{\gamma}\Big)^2,\qquad R=\max_i\|x_i\|,\qquad \gamma=\min_i\ y_i\,(w^{*\top}x_i)\ \ \text{with}\ \|w^*\|=1$$

Symbols: $w^*$ is any unit vector that separates the data (the bound is stated for a plane through the origin). $\gamma$ is the distance of the closest point from that plane. $R$ is how far the farthest point is from the origin.

**Worked example.** Class $+1$ at $(3,2)$ and $(-1,4)$, class $-1$ at $(2,-1)$ and $(-3,-2)$. The unit vector $w^*=(0,1)$ separates them (no bias). Find the perceptron mistake bound.

1. $w^*=(0,1)$ has length 1. The plane is the line $x_2=0$. The $+$ points are above it and the $-$ points below.
2. Margins $y\,w^{*\top}x$: $1\cdot2=2$, $1\cdot4=4$, $(-1)(-1)=1$, $(-1)(-2)=2$. The smallest is $\gamma=1$.
3. Lengths $\|x\|$: $\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13}$, $\sqrt{1+16}=\sqrt{17}$, $\sqrt{4+1}=\sqrt5$, $\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13}$. The largest is $R=\sqrt{17}\approx4.12$.
4. Bound $=(R/\gamma)^2=(\sqrt{17}/1)^2=17$.
5. So at most 17 updates happen, whatever order the points come in.

**Answer:** At most $(R/\gamma)^2=17$ mistakes. A bound, not an exact count: the real number can be smaller.

**Check yourself:** A separable data set has $R=5$ and $\gamma=0.5$. What is the mistake bound?

*Answer:* $(5/0.5)^2=10^2=100$.

scenes.title: A perceptron draws one straight line

steps.caption: A perceptron outputs sign(f), where f = w.x + b. Here w = (2, 1) and b = -4, so the boundary f = 0 is the line 2x1 + x2 = 4. It crosses the axes at (2, 0) and (0, 4). The arrow w points toward the + side.
Point A = (1, 1): f = 2 + 1 - 4 = -1. Negative, so the output is -1 and A sits on the - side.
Point B = (3, 1): f = 6 + 1 - 4 = 3. Positive, so the output is +1.
Point C = (1, 3): f = 2 + 3 - 4 = 1. Positive, so the output is +1.
One straight line splits the plane into two half-planes. B and C are on the side that w points to, and A is on the other. A perceptron can only draw lines like this.
A perceptron with w = (1, -1) and b = 0. The line f = x1 - x2 = 0 splits the plane. The arrow w points toward the side predicted +1.
The + point (1, 3) should be +1, but f = 1 - 3 = -2. It sits on the wrong side, so y f = -2 is not positive. This is a mistake.
Update: w = w + y x = (1, -1) + 1 x (1, 3) = (2, 2), and b = 0 + 1 = 1. The dashed arrow is x, added to w.
The weight vector swings toward the point and the line moves. Now f(1,3) = 2 + 6 + 1 = 9. y f rose from -2 to 9, a rise of 11 = |x|^2 + 1 = 1 + 9 + 1.

scenes.title: Counting the parameters of a 2-3-1 network

steps.caption: A 2-3-1 network has 2 inputs, 3 hidden units and 1 output unit. Each arrow carries one weight and each non-input unit has one bias. Count the learnable parameters.

set.text: weights = arrows,  biases = one per unit

steps.caption: Layer 1: each of the 3 hidden units connects to both inputs, so there are 2 x 3 = 6 arrows, which is 6 weights.
Each hidden unit also has one bias: 3 more. Layer 1 has 6 + 3 = 9 parameters.
Layer 2: 3 arrows into the output are 3 weights, plus 1 bias for the output unit. That is 4 parameters.
Total = 9 + 4 = 13. There are 6 neurons, but neurons are not what we count. We count arrows and biases.

scenes.title: Stacked linear layers collapse into one

objects.text: h = W1 x,    y = W2 h    (identity activation)

steps.caption: Two layers with identity activation, which means no bend between them: h = W1 x and then y = W2 h. W1 is [[1, 1], [1, -1]] and W2 is [1, 2].
Forward pass for x = (2, 1). h = (1x2 + 1x1, 1x2 - 1x1) = (3, 1). Then y = 1x3 + 2x1 = 5.
Multiply the matrices first: P = W2 W1 = [1(1) + 2(1), 1(1) + 2(-1)] = [3, -1]. Then P x = 3(2) - 1(1) = 5. The same answer from one layer.
Two linear layers are one linear layer with weights [3, -1]. Adding more linear layers adds no new power.

set.text: two linear layers = one linear layer

steps.caption: Put a ReLU (max of 0 and the value) on the hidden layer and take x = (1, 2). h = (3, -1) becomes (3, 0). Then y = 1x3 + 2x0 = 3. The single map P gives 3(1) - 1(2) = 1. They differ, so the bend breaks the collapse.

scenes.title: Two hidden units draw two lines and the output combines them

steps.caption: XOR: the points (0, 1) and (1, 0) are class +, and (0, 0) and (1, 1) are class -. One line cannot split them. Two hidden threshold units, one output unit, can.
Hidden unit 1 fires when x1 - x2 > 0.5. Its line cuts off the corner (1, 0). Over the four inputs h1 is 0, 0, 1, 0.
Hidden unit 2 fires when x2 - x1 > 0.5. Its line cuts off the corner (0, 1). Over the four inputs h2 is 0, 1, 0, 0.
The output unit says yes when h1 + h2 > 0.5, which means at least one hidden unit fired. The outputs are 0, 1, 1, 0: exactly XOR.

set.text: yes if either hidden unit fires

steps.caption: Picture it: the two lines make a strip between them. The - points (0, 0) and (1, 1) sit inside the strip and the + points sit outside, on opposite sides. The output unit joins the two outer half-planes.

set.text: the - points sit in the strip between the lines

scenes.title: Margin and radius give the perceptron mistake bound

steps.caption: A separable data set: + at (3, 2) and (-1, 4), - at (2, -1) and (-3, -2). The unit vector w* = (0, 1) with no bias separates them: the line x2 = 0 has the + points above and the - points below.
The margin is how far the nearest point is from that line, measured along w*. The distances are 2, 4, 1 and 2, so gamma = 1. The nearest point is (2, -1).
R is the length of the longest input vector. The lengths are sqrt(13), sqrt(17), sqrt(5) and sqrt(13), so R = sqrt(17), about 4.12. The circle of radius R holds every point.
Mistake bound = (R / gamma)^2 = (sqrt(17) / 1)^2 = 17.
So the perceptron makes at most 17 updates on this data, whatever order it sees the points. A wider margin or a smaller R means fewer mistakes.

set.text: at most 17 mistakes, in any order
